name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 18 July 1970

clue.text: High water is not con fined to Leap Years

blocks.clueFragment: High water is not con fined to Leap Years
blocks.note: surface reading: some flood that does not only happen in the years with an extra February day
setter's reading: a leap is a bound, so these are the seasons named after bounding, and this high water is not tied to that season at all

explanation.surface: A puzzle about floods that are not restricted to leap years.
explanation.walkthrough: A spring tide has nothing to do with the season: it comes twice a month at new and full moon, so it is not confined to spring, the leaping time.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest tides of the lunar cycle, at new and full moon, carry this name and bring the greatest rise in sea level.

clue.text: Sticks to the selectively taxed county

blocks.note: first meaning: walking poles or rods
second meaning: the short form of Staffordshire, an English county, with a nod to a tax on employees

explanation.surface: Someone clinging to an English county singled out for taxation.
explanation.walkthrough: Britain's Selective Employment Tax (1966) was charged per employee, so it taxed staff; Staffs is the usual abbreviation for Staffordshire, an English Midlands county.
explanation.definitionFit: Poles carried for walking are staffs, and the standard postal abbreviation for Staffordshire spells the same word.

clue.text: Follow the beaten track?

blocks.note: surface reading: walk along a well-worn path
setter's reading: what a defeated army does is fall back along the route it came

explanation.surface: Advice to stick to the well-trodden path.
explanation.walkthrough: The beaten track is not a worn path but the road taken by those who have been beaten in battle.
explanation.definitionFit: An army that has lost a battle withdraws, falling back from the enemy, which is the military sense of the verb.

clue.text: It's South of the Bor dor — and not hitchhiker country

definitions.text: It's South of the Bor dor

blocks.note: nor is a word of negation, standing for not
a hitchhiker thumbs lifts, so is a thumber
a land is a country

explanation.surface: A county just below the Scottish border where nobody will give you a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bor dor' is a printing slip for Border, the line between England and Scotland. NORTHUMBERLAND is England's most northerly county, just south of it.
explanation.definitionFit: This English county lies immediately south of the Anglo-Scottish boundary, so it sits just below the Border.

clue.text: Felix returned it without a word

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: Felix the Cat is the famous cartoon character
taken as written

explanation.surface: Felix the cat gave something back without saying anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Something understood or implied rather than spoken aloud is unstated, communicated silently.

clue.text: Curfews not ringing tonight in the Gym?

definitions.text: Curfews not ringing tonight in the Gym?

blocks.note: surface reading: echoes the poem 'Curfew Must Not Ring Tonight', about a bell kept silent
setter's reading: bells that make no sound are silent bells, and those found in a gym are weights

explanation.surface: A misplaced line from a Victorian poem about a curfew bell, relocated to a gymnasium.
explanation.walkthrough: A curfew was announced by a bell; a bell that cannot ring is mute, and mute bells are the iron weights of the gym.
explanation.definitionFit: Short bars with weighted ends, lifted for exercise, take their name from silent bell-ringing practice apparatus.

clue.text: Crazy fliers

blocks.note: first meaning: mad, as in having ... in the belfry
second meaning: winged mammals that fly at night

explanation.surface: Reckless pilots.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally someone mad is called this, and the nocturnal winged mammals share the same spelling.

clue.text: His speciality love — in a mist? That's about right

indicators.note: the letters placed in the phrase sit inside it rather than beside it

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A lover moves through a romantic haze, and that sounds about correct.
explanation.walkthrough: Love-in-a-mist is also a flower. The O and R go inside A MIST, after its M.
explanation.definitionFit: A person devoted to romance and lovemaking, whose speciality is love, is a lover or gallant.

clue.text: The main vessels used in the kitchen

definitions.text: The main vessels used in the kitchen

blocks.note: surface reading: the principal pots and pans; setter's reading: the main is the sea, so these are ships
the same word also names cooking pots that cook food with vapour

explanation.surface: The chief pots a cook relies on.
explanation.walkthrough: The main is the old word for the open sea, so 'main vessels' are ships powered by boilers; the same word is a kind of cooking pot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships driven by boilers and pans that cook food over boiling water share one name.

clue.text: Venator, when fully instructed on the right lines?

definitions.text: Venator, when fully instructed on the right lines?

blocks.note: surface reading: Latin for hunter, and the huntsman in Izaak Walton's 1653 book on fishing who is taught by Piscator

blocks.clueFragment: fully instructed on the right lines
blocks.note: setter's reading: once fully taught to fish with line and rod he would be a perfect fisherman, which is that book's title

explanation.surface: A Latin-named pupil who has finally been taught properly.
explanation.walkthrough: Compleat is the archaic spelling of complete; lines are fishing lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Walton's classic book of 1653 is titled after the perfect fisherman, whom the pupil Venator is trained to become.

clue.text: Change one's ego?

blocks.note: first meaning: to modify
second meaning: completes the phrase for a second self

explanation.surface: A question about whether a person can transform their sense of self.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is a phrase to complete rather than a straight synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To modify something is the verb sense, and a second self is called an alter ego, from Latin for other.

clue.text: Officer's chest-of drawers is inlaid with gold

indicators.note: furniture inlaid with a material has it set into its surface, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a commode is an ornate chest of drawers
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A naval man's chest of drawers decorated with gold inlay.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for gold is heraldic language, common in crosswords; a commode here is the antique chest, not the bedside toilet chair.
explanation.definitionFit: A naval officer ranking above captain holds this title, as does the head of a yacht club.

clue.text: Worry about the lady in the flood

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps around the next

blocks.note: to fret is to worry
the lady is she

explanation.surface: Anxiety about a woman caught in rising water.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden rush of fresh water into a river or the sea after rain or snowmelt is a small spate.

clue.text: A religious calling

blocks.note: surface reading: a vocation to the priesthood or a holy order
setter's reading: calling as naming, so the church ceremony at which a child is given a name

explanation.surface: A vocation to the ministry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian sacrament of christening, when an infant is sprinkled with water and given a name, is a naming done by the church.

clue.text: A penny in the black his first aim?

definitions.text: A penny in the black his first aim?

blocks.note: surface reading: being a penny in credit, out of debt
setter's reading: the Penny Black, the world's first postage stamp of 1840, is a prize for a philatelist to acquire

explanation.surface: A careful saver whose first goal is to be a penny in credit.
explanation.walkthrough: In the black means in credit, but the Penny Black was the first adhesive postage stamp, issued in Britain in 1840.
explanation.definitionFit: A philatelist, a hobbyist who gathers postage issues, would prize the rare first adhesive one above all.

clue.text: Cantor has a lot of trouble in the choir

indicators.note: letters in trouble are thrown into disorder and must be sorted out again

blocks.note: taken as written
a lot is the word lot

explanation.surface: A synagogue singer runs into difficulty during choir practice.
explanation.walkthrough: A cantor leads singing in a synagogue, which makes the surface plausible; the definition is the loose 'in the choir', naming a voice part found there.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest female singing voice is one of the standard parts of a choir, alongside soprano, tenor and bass.

clue.text: Messy eaters

blocks.note: surface reading: people who eat sloppily
setter's reading: those who eat in the mess, the dining room of military commanders

explanation.surface: People who leave crumbs everywhere at the table.
explanation.walkthrough: A mess is a military dining hall, and the officers' mess is where commissioned ranks dine.
explanation.definitionFit: Commissioned ranks in the armed forces take their meals together in their own dining hall, called a mess.

clue.text: It's not a refrain for breaking into the "Let's be buddies" routine

indicators.note: something breaking comes apart, so the words are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: A denial that some catchy chorus is the start of a friendly overture.
explanation.definitionFit: Becoming friendly and chummy with others, especially former enemies, is the behaviour of acting like buddies.

clue.text: The tail-less dog of Whitefriars

indicators.note: without a tail means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: the Alsatian is the British name for the German shepherd dog

explanation.surface: A dog with no tail belonging to a London friary.
explanation.walkthrough: Alsatia was the slang name for Whitefriars in London, a former sanctuary where debtors and criminals hid from the law.
explanation.definitionFit: The old district of Whitefriars, a lawless sanctuary in seventeenth-century London, was nicknamed after the disputed border province.

clue.text: "While the chaffinch sings on the — bough" (Browning)

definitions.text: "While the chaffinch sings on the — bough" (Browning)

blocks.clueFragment: "While the chaffinch sings on the — bough"
blocks.note: a line from Robert Browning's 'Home-Thoughts, from Abroad' with one word missing
names the poet so the solver can supply the missing word from the poem

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Victorian poem about an English spring, with a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem continues 'In England — now!'; the missing word describes the bough as belonging to a fruit-tree plot.
explanation.definitionFit: A plantation of fruit trees such as apples or pears is where the chaffinch perches in Browning's line.

clue.text: In Rome it initially preceded its three alphabetical predecessors

definitions.text: In Rome it initially preceded its three alphabetical predecessors

blocks.note: surface reading: the Roman state

blocks.clueFragment: initially preceded its three alphabetical predecessors
blocks.note: setter's reading: in the Roman motto SPQR the S, its initial, came before P, Q and R, the three letters before S in the alphabet

explanation.surface: A riddle about the order of letters in an ancient Roman inscription.
explanation.walkthrough: SPQR stands for Senatus Populusque Romanus, 'the Senate and People of Rome'.
explanation.definitionFit: The governing council of ancient Rome is the first word of the motto, its initial heading the inscription.

clue.text: Is Man so narrow minded?

blocks.note: first meaning: the Isle of Man is an island, so of an island
second meaning: inward-looking and intolerant of outside ideas

explanation.surface: A question whether mankind is intolerant.
explanation.walkthrough: Man here is the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland, not humankind.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to an island describes the Isle, and people cut off from outside views are figuratively parochial.

clue.text: He follows Peter and Bill to the Plume of Feathers

indicators.note: coming after means placing the first piece at the end

blocks.note: Peter Pan, J. M. Barrie's boy who never grew up
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man trails two friends to a pub called the Plume of Feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Plume of Feathers sounds like a pub name, but it is the definition: the word's original sense is a crest of feathers on a helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: Originally the tuft of plumes worn on a helmet, the word now means flamboyant style or flair.

clue.text: Assume there's one in the mail!

indicators.note: something in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the post is the mail
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Take it there is a letter waiting in the delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in the mail' sounds like a letter on its way; the exclamation mark dresses up a plain container clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To put forward as a basis for argument, taking it as given, is to postulate or suppose.

clue.text: Involves in ten unusual points of view

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: the three letters reordered
an angle is a point of view

explanation.surface: Someone drawn into ten odd perspectives.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensnare or draw something into a complicated situation is to tangle it up, catch it in a mesh.

clue.text: Animal backed to find a way to the Palace

indicators.note: backed means moved backwards, so the words are read from the end

blocks.note: taken as written
The Mall is the London avenue leading to Buckingham Palace

explanation.surface: A creature reversing to find its route to the royal residence.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of A plus MALL is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: The woolly South American beast of burden related to the camel is a creature, an animal.

clue.text: A pointed attempt in return for 6

indicators.note: something given in return goes back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: 6 refers to the answer at 6-across

explanation.surface: A sharp try at something, given back in exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: A number in a clue stands for the answer to that entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A try at something is a go or shot, and a thrust with a knife is literally pointed, so the attempt is sharp.

clue.text: It's over the line for the infantry game

blocks.note: foot soldiers are the infantry
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: Crossing the line, perhaps in a military sporting match.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is a railway line, not a line of troops or a touchline.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow crossing for walkers spans a railway track or river, carrying pedestrians across it.
